sections.contenu_markdown: Certain English verbs are systematically followed by a to-infinitive, never a gerund — a list worth memorising rather than deducing.

The verb 'intend' is always followed by a to-infinitive ('intend to do'), never by a gerund ('intend doing') or a past participle. Other common verbs in this group include: decide to, plan to, hope to, want to, agree to, promise to, refuse to.

sections.enonce_markdown: Complete: 'What do you intend ___ about the leaky pipes?'
sections.conclusion_markdown: "What do you intend to do about the leaky pipes?"

items.erreur_markdown: Using the gerund ('intend doing') by analogy with verbs like 'enjoy' or 'avoid', which do take a gerund.
items.pourquoi_faux: Not all verbs follow the same pattern: 'intend' specifically requires a to-infinitive, unlike 'enjoy doing' or 'avoid doing'.
items.correction_markdown: Memorise 'intend' as part of the to-infinitive group, distinct from the gerund group (enjoy, avoid, finish, mind...).

items_markdown: intend, decide, plan, hope, want, promise + to-infinitive
enjoy, avoid, finish, mind + gerund (different group)
